posts.topic: CLARITY Act markup targets mid-May amid bank pushback
posts.source_headline: CLARITY Act Breakthrough: Senator Tillis Backs Markup and Says Stablecoin Disputes Are Resolved
posts.x_post: U.S. banks are lobbying to delay the CLARITY Act even as Senator Tillis locks in a mid-May markup date. The stablecoin yield standoff is resolved: passive rewards banned, activity-based rewards tied to payments and transfers kept. DeFi provisions still contested. My read: $317 billion in stablecoin supply accumulated without asking banks for permission. The bill dying in committee will not change that.
posts.substack_note:
My read: The CLARITY Act finally has a markup date. Week of May 11, pending Senator Tillis's committee schedule. The stablecoin yield compromise took three months to reach: passive holding rewards banned, activity-based rewards tied to payments and transfers permitted.

Now the loudest lobby for delay is U.S. banks.

I find this strange. The GENIUS Act already created a federal stablecoin framework last July. $317 billion in stablecoin supply circulates today. Visa settled $4.6 billion on its network this quarter alone. The banks are not blocking a future — they are trying to slow a present they did not build.

The real constraint is temporal. If the bill does not clear committee before Congress shifts to campaign season, it dies with this session. That window is roughly eight weeks.

If the CLARITY Act fails, does stablecoin expansion accelerate offshore, or does it simply wait for the next political cycle?

posts.topic: Coinbase CUSHY tokenizes stablecoin credit for institutions
posts.source_headline: Coinbase's asset manager to offer stablecoin credit fund with tokenized share class
posts.x_post: Northern Trust is now administering a fund that settles on Solana. Coinbase's CUSHY, a tokenized stablecoin credit fund for institutions, delivers yield from onchain lending across Ethereum, Solana, and Base, with shares usable as DeFi collateral around the clock. Invesco, $2 trillion under management, adopted the same Superstate FundOS infrastructure. My read: TradFi is not adopting DeFi selectively. It is adopting the rails and calling it a credit strategy.
posts.substack_note:
My take: I have watched the 'institutional DeFi' narrative for years. Mostly it was slideware. CUSHY, Coinbase's tokenized stablecoin credit fund announced April 30, feels structurally different.

Northern Trust is administering a fund that trades 24/7 on Solana. That is not a crypto headline. It is a custody desk decision. Invesco, $2 trillion AUM, adopted the same Superstate FundOS infrastructure. Yield comes from three sources: asset-based lending to crypto-native and traditional borrowers, digital credit instruments, and tokenization incentives.

That last source is temporary. Tokenization incentives will not last. But the first two are real credit exposure with real counterparties.

For MENA investors, Gulf sovereign wealth is already circling digital assets. The question is whether regional allocators reach this fund class before the Western first-mover window closes.

Is CUSHY the product that finally makes institutional stablecoin yield legible to a traditional LP in Abu Dhabi or Riyadh?

posts.topic: Rain buys Arabic crypto media to own MENA conversion funnel
posts.source_headline: Abu Dhabi's Rain Financial acquires Saudi-based Digital Ma'arefa
posts.x_post: Rain, the Gulf's first licensed crypto exchange with $11 billion in total trading volume, acquired Digital Ma'arefa, the Arabic-language financial media network with 1 million followers. Deal closed March 30. The move is not about content. My read: the exchange that controls what one million Arabic-speaking investors read before they trade owns the conversion funnel at every step.
posts.substack_note:
My take: Rain is MENA's first regulated crypto exchange. Two million users. $11 billion in lifetime trading volume. Licensed in Bahrain, approved by ADGM.

On March 30, they acquired Digital Ma'arefa, the Arabic-language financial media company behind Finance Memo and Crypto Memo, with one million followers built over five years. Abdullah Mashat, the brand's most trusted voice, joins as Managing Director.

I have watched how Arabic-speaking investors navigate financial media for years. Trust is scarce. English-language crypto content rarely translates culturally. What Rain bought is not a newsletter. It is the decision environment that precedes a trade.

The expansion roadmap names Turkey and Pakistan as next markets. That combination — Bahrain headquarters, ADGM approval, Saudi media, Pakistan ambition — maps almost exactly to where remittance-to-investment conversion is most underserved.

What does vertical integration from information to custody look like at real scale in Arabic?

posts.topic: Visa stablecoin settlement hits $7B across nine blockchains
posts.source_headline: Visa Accelerates Stablecoin Momentum: Adding Five Blockchains for Settlement
posts.x_post: Visa's annualized stablecoin settlement run rate hit $7B on April 29, up 50% in one quarter, now across nine blockchains. 130+ card programs live in 50+ countries. My read: Visa is treating stablecoins as permanent settlement infrastructure, not a pilot. The rail is being built while the train is already moving.
posts.substack_note:
There's a data point in Visa's April 29 announcement that deserves more attention than the blockchain count.

$7 billion annualized settlement run rate, up 50% in a single quarter, across nine blockchains, with 130+ card programs in 50+ countries. That is not a pilot. Pilots don't grow 50% per quarter.

I've been watching this space closely. The interesting part isn't the volume. It's that Visa — a company built entirely on owning the settlement layer — is accelerating stablecoin adoption rather than resisting it. They're becoming the brand on top of a permissionless rail.

My read: the network that once extracted margin from correspondent banking is now racing to own programmable settlement before someone else does. Whether that's strategy or an existential hedge is genuinely unclear to me.

What changes when the settlement layer is permissionless but Visa's name is still on the card?

posts.topic: World Bank reclassifies Pakistan from South Asia to MENAAP
posts.source_headline: Pakistan's New Geographic Designation Brings Complications
posts.x_post: The World Bank reclassified Pakistan from South Asia to MENAAP, effective fiscal year 2026, moving $20 billion in programming with it. My read: this is not symbolic. ADB, MSCI, Bloomberg, and the Islamic Development Bank tend to follow the World Bank's lead. When the data taxonomy shifts, lending frameworks, sector benchmarks, and investment mandates follow.
posts.substack_note:
There's a story buried in the World Bank's April 2026 metadata update that most outlets treated as bureaucratic housekeeping.

Pakistan has been moved from the South Asia regional group to MENAAP, a new designation covering Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. Effective fiscal year 2026.

I find this genuinely consequential, and not for symbolic reasons. World Bank regions are not just labels. They carry vice presidencies, country directors, sector teams, regional trust funds, and lending architecture. When Pakistan moves into MENAAP, $20 billion in World Bank programming gets redesigned around Gulf-style development playbooks rather than South Asian ones.

The second-order effect is what matters: ADB, MSCI, Bloomberg, and the Islamic Development Bank typically follow the World Bank's categorization. Pakistan's startup ecosystem already has one foot in Dubai. This accelerates the other.

Whether this deepens Pakistan's strategic access to Gulf capital, or just deepens dependency on Gulf capital cycles, is the question I can't answer sitting in the UAE.

posts.topic: MENA fintech captures 46% of Q1 2026 funding despite 37% drop
posts.source_headline: Middle East Fintech Investors Pivot To Resilient Local Infrastructure Amid Regional Turmoil: Analysis
posts.x_post: MENA startup funding fell to $941M in Q1 2026, down 37% year-on-year. Fintech captured 46% of every dollar deployed. My read: when Gulf capital gets nervous, it does not exit fintech. It consolidates inside it.
posts.substack_note:
The Q1 2026 MENA funding numbers tell two stories that most coverage is conflating.

Story one: $941 million in total startup funding, down 37% year-on-year. Geopolitical stress around the Strait of Hormuz is eroding investor confidence. That part is accurate.

Story two: fintech captured 46% of every dollar deployed in the region. Not despite the turmoil. Because of it.

I've been thinking about why this pattern holds. When regional instability rises, remittance volumes increase and demand for local financial infrastructure deepens. Investors who understand this lean in rather than pull back.

Fintech in MENA right now is not a growth bet. It is an infrastructure bet.

My hypothesis: the next wave of MENA fintech winners will be built on deals made during this quiet quarter, not the loud years. Capital concentrated under pressure finds the strongest structures.

What does the next dominant MENA fintech category look like?

posts.topic: Trump hears Iran strike options as diplomat track fails
posts.source_headline: Scoop: Commanders to brief Trump on new Iran military options Thursday
posts.x_post: CENTCOM briefs Trump today on three Iran strike options: infrastructure attacks, seizing the Strait of Hormuz, or a special forces raid on Iran's enriched uranium stockpiles. The 60-day congressional war deadline is approaching. Pakistan's PM spent the morning calling Tehran and Riyadh. My read: when generals are briefing and brokers are calling, only one track is gaining ground.
posts.substack_note:
My read: Two things happened today that cannot coexist much longer.

Pakistan's PM spent the morning on calls to Tehran and Riyadh — the last visible movement on the diplomatic track. Then Axios broke the scoop: CENTCOM will brief Trump on three Iran strike options. Infrastructure attacks. Seizing the Strait of Hormuz. A special forces raid on Iran's enriched uranium stockpile. Congress's 60-day war deadline is approaching and wants an answer.

Trump told Axios on Wednesday that the naval blockade is 'somewhat more effective than the bombing.' That is not the language of someone who expects talks to succeed.

The Hormuz angle is where I have been paying the most attention. Every week that strait is constrained applies direct pressure to Gulf energy pricing and MENA trade flows. UAE and Saudi Arabia feel this in their growth numbers, not just their headlines.

At what point does 'maintain pressure' become 'execute'?

posts.topic: MENA Q1 VC drops 37% but fintech captures 46%
posts.source_headline: MENA startup funding slips to $941 million in Q1 2026 amid heightened geopolitical risk
posts.x_post: MENA venture fell 37% year-on-year in Q1 2026 to $941M, the Hormuz blockade alone killing February sentiment with the month closing at just $326.6M. But fintech captured 46% of all capital deployed, 25 startups pulling the largest share even as broader deal-making cratered. My read: geopolitical shock concentrates MENA capital, it doesn't disperse it. When macro goes sideways, smart money narrows to the one sector with clear revenue models.
posts.substack_note:
My read: the headline number misleads.

MENA startup funding hit $941M in Q1 2026, down 37% year-on-year. The Hormuz blockade hit mid-February and the back half of the quarter collapsed — February alone closed at $326.6M as the conflict deepened. UAE took $625.8M across 46 deals. Saudi Arabia managed $156.7M across 57. Egypt: $86M across 12.

But fintech captured 46% of total capital. Twenty-five startups raised more than any other sector in the region combined.

I've watched this pattern repeat: when MENA macro wobbles, investors don't exit — they concentrate. Fintech wins by default because it has what most of the stack lacks: predictable unit economics and regulatory tailwind from governments that desperately need digital payments infrastructure to keep working.

The harder question isn't why fintech held up. It's what the sector looks like if this conflict runs another two quarters.

posts.topic: World Bank moves Pakistan into MENA regional grouping
posts.source_headline: Pakistan's New Geographic Designation Brings Complications
posts.x_post: The World Bank moved Pakistan from South Asia to MENAAP. The region's population jumped from 519M to 813M, per-capita GDP fell over 30%, and Pakistan is now the demographic anchor of a bloc it was not officially part of last year. My read: this formalizes where Pakistan's capital flows have always pointed, toward Gulf debt, Gulf remittances, and Gulf sovereign risk.
posts.substack_note:
My take: a World Bank administrative update is doing something quietly consequential.

Pakistan was reclassified from South Asia into MENAAP — Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, Pakistan — effective July 2025. MENAAP's population jumped from 519 million to 813 million overnight. Per-capita GDP fell more than 30%. Pakistan is now the largest demographic weight in a grouping it never formally belonged to.

I find this interesting because it formalizes what's been economically true for years. Pakistan's remittance flows, diaspora capital, and sovereign debt structures have been Gulf-oriented for a long time. The World Bank is catching up to where the money already goes.

The complications are real: IMF programs calibrate to regional peers, development lending follows group comparisons, and trade classification shapes market access terms.

Whether this opens a door to Gulf-adjacent capital flows or just inherits the region's geopolitical volatility — I'm genuinely unsure. What's your read?

posts.topic: Pakistan PM contacts Iran and Saudi Arabia April 30
posts.source_headline: Pakistan tries to broker US-Iran deal but prospects keep slipping away
posts.x_post: Pakistan hosted US-Iran talks on April 11-12. Trump then cancelled the follow-up, calling it 'too much work,' and Iran's position fractured. Today, Shehbaz Sharif is calling both Tehran and Riyadh simultaneously. My read: Pakistan's diplomatic window is real but closing fast, and every stalled week raises the domestic cost of being the neutral venue while Hormuz eats into the current account.
posts.substack_note:
My take: Pakistan has found leverage — and it's not clear how long it holds.

Islamabad hosted US-Iran talks on April 11-12. Trump then called the follow-up 'too much work' and cancelled the Witkoff-Kushner visit. Iran's position fractured further. Today — April 30 — PM Shehbaz Sharif is calling both Tehran and Riyadh simultaneously, trying to keep a process alive that neither principal seems fully committed to.

What strikes me about this: the same Hormuz conflict damaging Pakistan's trade routes and current account is also what's giving Islamabad diplomatic utility. Saudi support is reportedly steadying the balance of payments. Tehran needs a back-channel. Washington needs a venue. Pakistan is absorbing both shocks while positioning itself as the honest broker.

The World Bank just formally moved Pakistan into MENAAP. The geopolitical logic was already there before the paperwork caught up.

The harder question: is Pakistan building durable diplomatic capital here, or taking on reputational risk for an outcome entirely outside its control?

posts.topic: Meta routes creator payments through USDC via Stripe
posts.source_headline: Meta Launches USDC Stablecoin Creator Payouts on Solana and Polygon via Stripe
posts.x_post: Meta just turned 3+ billion users into a live stablecoin settlement network. USDC on Solana and Polygon, routed through Stripe, paying creators in Colombia and the Philippines, two of the world's highest-fee dollar conversion corridors. My read: the 'crypto moment' everyone waited for was not a DeFi protocol. It was a payroll function quietly embedded inside a social app.
posts.substack_note:
My take: Meta's stablecoin rollout is being framed as a crypto story. It isn't.

Four years after Libra collapsed under regulatory pressure, Meta didn't launch a new coin. It plugged into Circle's USDC and Stripe's infrastructure and began paying creators in Colombia and the Philippines. Two markets where converting USD payouts to local currency routinely costs 5 to 7% per transaction.

I've watched stablecoin adoption for several years, and the pattern is consistent: the breakthrough never arrives when a blockchain startup announces a product. It arrives when a 3.2 billion-user platform quietly converts its payroll function into a settlement rail.

The question I keep returning to: does Meta expand this to advertising disbursements? If brand payments follow creator payments, you have a stablecoin network processing commercial-scale volumes before most analysts notice.

posts.topic: UAE captures 66% of MENA's contracting Q1 2026 funding

Saudi Arabia pulled in $156.7 million across 57 deals. My read: MENA's innovation capital is not slowing. It is concentrating. The Hormuz disruptions accelerated the flight to certainty, and UAE is where certainty lives.
posts.substack_note:
My read: when total MENA startup funding falls 37% year-on-year, the instinct is to call it a regional slowdown. The data says something more specific.

UAE raised $625.8 million in Q1 2026, capturing 66% of the region's entire $941 million. Saudi Arabia ran 57 deals but raised only $156.7 million. Egypt pulled in $86 million across 12 transactions.

I'm based in the UAE, and I've seen this pattern before: when regional risk spikes, capital doesn't leave MENA. It relocates within MENA. Iran's Hormuz blockade created genuine uncertainty across seaborne logistics. Investors still wanted regional exposure. They just wanted it from a jurisdiction with regulatory clarity and no proximity to the disruption.

Fintech led at 46% of total funding. That's what investors trust when nervous: clear revenue models, not speculative bets.

What does this concentration mean for founders building from Cairo or Riyadh? I'm still working through that.

posts.topic: Pakistan opens land corridor into blockaded Iran

posts.substack_note:
My read: Pakistan opened 6 overland trade routes into Iran today while thousands of containers sit stranded at Karachi port under the US Hormuz blockade. Iranian FM Araghchi is back in Islamabad, his second visit this month, for talks with PM Shehbaz and army chief Asim Munir.

posts.topic: Visa stablecoin settlement doubles to $7B run rate
posts.source_headline: Visa (V) expands stablecoin settlement network as volume hits $7 billion run rate
posts.x_post: Visa's stablecoin settlement hit a $7 billion annualized run rate this week, double the $3.5 billion recorded in December. The network now covers 9 blockchains and 130 card programs across 50 countries after adding 5 chains in a single announcement. My read: Visa is not competing with stablecoin rails. It is inserting itself as the clearing layer above them, and that position is very hard to displace.
posts.substack_note:
My read: Visa's stablecoin settlement volume hit $7 billion annualized this week, double its December 2025 rate, across 9 blockchains, 130 card programs, and 50 countries. This is live transaction volume, not a forecast.

I was skeptical for a while that traditional networks would move fast enough to matter here. This week shifts my view. Visa isn't defending turf, it's occupying the clearing layer above whichever rails survive. That's a strategically different posture from what most traditional payments incumbents are doing.

The incumbents who've spent decades building enterprise trust have structural advantages the original stablecoin thesis underestimated: networks, compliance relationships, counterparty credibility.

Is this Visa genuinely capturing the stablecoin era, or building one more integration layer that a truly decentralised settlement stack will eventually route around?

posts.topic: Meta relaunches stablecoin creator payments via USDC/Stripe
posts.source_headline: Meta (META) starts stablecoin payout to creators in Circle's USDC on Polygon, Solana via Stripe
posts.x_post: Meta killed its own stablecoin project, Diem, in January 2022 rather than fight regulators for the right to issue currency. Four years later, the replacement uses USDC not Diem, Stripe not Novi, Polygon and Solana not a proprietary chain, and launches in Colombia and Philippines, two of the world's largest remittance corridors. My read: the $293 billion stablecoin market built itself in Meta's absence, and Meta just quietly re-entered as a distribution layer.
posts.substack_note: I keep thinking about how quietly Meta walked back into the stablecoin conversation. In January 2022, Diem was sold off and pronounced dead — a generational ambition to issue private currency, ended without a fight. Four years later, the same company is paying creators in USDC, on Polygon and Solana, through Stripe, in Colombia and the Philippines. The $293B stablecoin market grew without them, and now they are entering as plumbing, not as the protagonist. My read: this is what conceding the issuance war but winning the distribution war looks like. The interesting question is whether the next layer down — wallets, remittance UX, fiat off-ramps — is actually the higher-margin layer all along. Curious how others are reading this. Are we underestimating what 'distribution-only' fintech looks like at Meta scale?
